passages.passageHtml:
"Society in every state is a blessing, but government even in its best state is but a necessary evil; in its worst state an intolerable one; for when we suffer, or are exposed to the same miseries by a government, which we might expect in a country without government, our calamity is heightened by reflecting that we furnish the means by which we suffer. Government, like dress, is the badge of lost innocence; the palaces of kings are built on the ruins of the bowers of paradise. For were the impulses of conscience clear, uniform, and irresistibly obeyed, man would need no other lawgiver; but that not being the case, he finds it necessary to surrender up a part of his property to furnish means for the protection of the rest; and this he is induced to do by the same prudence which in every other case advises him out of two evils to choose the least. Wherefore, security being the true design and end of government, it unanswerably follows that whatever form thereof appears most likely to ensure it to us, with the least expense and greatest benefit, is preferable to all others."

"I draw my idea of the form of government from a principle in nature, which no art can overturn, viz. that the more simple any thing is, the less liable it is to be disordered; and the easier repaired when disordered; and with this maxim in view, I offer a few remarks on the so much boasted constitution of England. That it was noble for the dark and slavish times in which it was erected, is granted. When the world was over run with tyranny the least remove therefrom was a glorious rescue. But that it is imperfect, subject to convulsions, and incapable of producing what it seems to promise, is easily demonstrated."

My own sex, I hope, will excuse me, if I treat them like rational creatures, instead of flattering their FASCINATING graces, and viewing them as if they were in a state of perpetual childhood, unable to stand alone. I earnestly wish to point out in what true dignity and human happiness consists—I wish to persuade women to endeavour to acquire strength, both of mind and body, and to convince them, that the soft phrases, susceptibility of heart, delicacy of sentiment, and refinement of taste, are almost synonymous with epithets of weakness, and that those beings who are only the objects of pity and that kind of love, which has been termed its sister, will soon become objects of contempt.

Dismissing then those pretty feminine phrases, which the men condescendingly use to soften our slavish dependence, and despising that weak elegancy of mind, exquisite sensibility, and sweet docility of manners, supposed to be the sexual characteristics of the weaker vessel, I wish to show that elegance is inferior to virtue, that the first object of laudable ambition is to obtain a character as a human being, regardless of the distinction of sex; and that secondary views should be brought to this simple touchstone.

After the Egyptian and Indian, the Greek and Roman, the Teuton and Mongolian, the Negro is a sort of seventh son, born with a veil, and gifted with second-sight in this American world, a world which yields him no true self-consciousness, but only lets him see himself through the revelation of the other world. It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one's self through the eyes of others, of measuring one's soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity. One ever feels his twoness, an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings; two warring ideals in one dark body, whose dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder.

The history of the American Negro is the history of this strife, this longing to attain self-conscious manhood, to merge his double self into a better and truer self. In this merging he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost. He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa. He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world. He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American, without being cursed and spit upon by his fellows, without having the doors of Opportunity closed roughly in his face.

How does it become a man to behave toward the American government today? I answer that he cannot without disgrace be associated with it. I cannot for an instant recognize that political organization as my government which is the slave's government also.

All men recognize the right of revolution; that is, the right to refuse allegiance to and to resist the government, when its tyranny or its inefficiency are great and unendurable. But almost all say that such is not the case now. But such was the case, they think, in the Revolution of '75. If one were to tell me that this was a bad government because it taxed certain foreign commodities brought to its ports, it is most probable that I should not make an ado about it, for I can do without them: all machines have their friction; and possibly this does enough good to counter-balance the evil. At any rate, it is a great evil to make a stir about it. But when the friction comes to have its machine, and oppression and robbery are organized, I say, let us not have such a machine any longer. In other words, when a sixth of the population of a nation which has undertaken to be the refuge of liberty are slaves, and a whole country is unjustly overrun and conquered by a foreign army, and subjected to military law, I think that it is not too soon for honest men to rebel and revolutionize. What makes this duty the more urgent is that fact, that the country so overrun is not our own, but ours is the invading army.

Paley, a common authority with many on moral questions, in his chapter on the "Duty of Submission to Civil Government," resolves all civil obligation into expediency; and he proceeds to say, "that so long as the interest of the whole society requires it, that is, so long as the established government cannot be resisted or changed without public inconvenience, it is the will of God that the established government be obeyed, and no longer."... Of this, he says, every man shall judge for himself. But Paley appears never to have contemplated those cases to which the rule of expediency does not apply, in which a people, as well as an individual, must do justice, cost what it may. If I have unjustly wrested a plank from a drowning man, I must restore it to him though I drown myself. This, according to Paley, would be inconvenient. But he that would save his life, in such a case, shall lose it. This people must cease to hold slaves, and to make war on Mexico, though it cost them their existence as a people.

It is in vain to say that enlightened statesmen will be able to adjust these clashing interests, and render them all subservient to the public good. Enlightened statesmen will not always be at the helm. Nor, in many cases, can such an adjustment be made at all without taking into view indirect and remote considerations, which will rarely prevail over the immediate interest which one party may find in disregarding the rights of another or the good of the whole.

The inference to which we are brought is, that the CAUSES of faction cannot be removed, and that relief is only to be sought in the means of controlling its EFFECTS.

If a faction consists of less than a majority, relief is supplied by the republican principle, which enables the majority to defeat its sinister views by regular vote... When a majority is included in a faction, the form of popular government, on the other hand, enables it to sacrifice to its ruling passion or interest both the public good and the rights of other citizens.

From this view of the subject it may be concluded that a pure democracy, by which I mean a society consisting of a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government in person, can admit of no cure for the mischiefs of faction... Hence it is that such democracies have ever been spectacles of turbulence and contention; have ever been found incompatible with personal security or the rights of property; and have in general been as short in their lives as they have been violent in their deaths.

A republic, by which I mean a government in which the scheme of representation takes place, opens a different prospect, and promises the cure for which we are seeking.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of the passage?

options.A: To argue that all forms of government are equally flawed, and that anarchy is the only rational alternative to tyranny
options.B: To demonstrate that the English constitution, despite its historical value, fails because its complexity makes it less effective than simpler governments
options.C: To convince readers that government is a punishment for human wickedness, and that security should be the only measure of a good government
options.D: To compare the English constitution unfavorably with absolute monarchies, which at least allow citizens to identify the source of their suffering

questions.explanationHtml: The author's main goal is to establish a principle (simpler governments are less disordered and easier to repair) and then apply it to judge the English constitution as flawed. He acknowledges the constitution was "noble" for its time but then argues it is "imperfect, subject to convulsions, and incapable" of delivering what it promises. The passage is not advocating anarchy (A); it explicitly says government is a necessary evil chosen as the lesser of two evils. While the author mentions human wickedness and security, those are supporting ideas, not the primary purpose (C). He notes one advantage of absolute governments (clarity of suffering) but does not aim to compare England unfavorably with them as a general claim (D); he calls absolute governments "the disgrace of human nature."

questions.questionHtml: The author addresses the claim that the English constitution is a "union of three powers reciprocally checking each other." How does he respond to this viewpoint?

options.A: He accepts the theory but argues that in practice, the commons is too weak to check the king, so the system collapses into monarchy
options.B: He rejects the claim as logically contradictory, arguing that the crown's control of financial rewards makes it the dominant power regardless of checks
options.C: He admits the system would work if the king were not hereditary, but since the king is born to power, the checks are meaningless
options.D: He agrees that the three powers exist but insists that the peers and commons are actually controlled by the same wealthy interests, making the checks an illusion

questions.explanationHtml: The author directly calls the "three powers checking each other" theory "farcical" and "a mere absurdity." He then shows why: the crown controls "places and pensions," giving it the "most weight," so the checks cannot stop it. He does not accept the theory even in theory (A) - he dismisses it as logically contradictory. He never claims heredity is the sole problem (C); his focus is on the crown's financial power. He also does not argue that wealthy interests control both peers and commons (D); that idea is not in this passage.

questions.questionHtml: Why does the author compare government to "dress" and "the badge of lost innocence"?

options.A: To suggest that government, like clothing, is an artificial invention that can be redesigned or discarded when it no longer serves its purpose
options.B: To imply that government is a necessary cover for human moral failure, but one that carries shame because it exists only due to our vice
options.C: To contrast the simplicity of natural society (where no government is needed) with the unnecessary complexity of modern political systems
options.D: To argue that just as clothing protects the body from the elements, government protects citizens from external threats like invasion or crime

questions.explanationHtml: The phrase "badge of lost innocence" echoes the religious concept of the Fall, implying shame and moral failure. Government is not a positive protector (D) but a cover for vice. The author says if conscience were perfect, "man would need no other lawgiver" - but since it is not, government is a humiliating necessity. While the author contrasts natural society with government (C), that is a broader theme, not the specific purpose of the dress/badge metaphor. Option A is partially true (government is artificial) but misses the element of shame and moral failure central to "lost innocence."

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of the passage?

options.A: To criticize men for using condescending language that traps women in a state of dependence, while also blaming women for willingly accepting flattery.
options.B: To argue that traditional feminine qualities like delicacy and sensitivity are not only useless but actively harmful, and that women should replace them with intellectual and moral strength.
options.C: To explain how the concept of "virtue" has been historically defined differently for men and women, and to propose a new unified standard.
options.D: To persuade women that seeking to inspire love in men is a waste of time, and that they should instead focus on becoming financially independent.

questions.explanationHtml:
The author states her goal directly: "I wish to persuade women to endeavour to acquire strength, both of mind and body" and "to show that elegance is inferior to virtue." Her primary purpose is not simply to criticize men or to explain history, but to convince women to abandon traditionally praised feminine traits (delicacy, sensitivity) in favor of rational and moral strength. Answer B captures this core persuasive argument.

Why A is incorrect: While the author does criticize men's language and notes women's acceptance of flattery, these are supporting points, not the main purpose. The central goal is to change women's behavior, not just assign blame.

Why C is incorrect: The passage makes no historical comparison of how virtue was defined for each sex in the past. This answer introduces content not found in the excerpt.

Why D is incorrect: Although the author mentions elsewhere that women are taught to "inspire love," this excerpt does not mention financial independence. The focus here is on strength of character and virtue, not economic matters.

questions.questionHtml: An opponent might argue that qualities like "delicacy of sentiment" and "sweet docility of manners" are precisely what make women virtuous and admirable. How does Wollstonecraft respond to this viewpoint in the passage?

options.A: She agrees that these qualities have some value but argues they have been exaggerated by men to keep women weak, so they should be practiced in moderation.
options.B: She dismisses the opposition without directly addressing it, focusing instead on describing the negative effects of male flattery.
options.C: She redefines those very qualities as forms of weakness that inevitably lead to contempt, not admiration, and therefore cannot be true virtues.
options.D: She claims that men who praise these qualities are insincere, and that women who display them are secretly manipulative and cunning.

questions.explanationHtml:
Wollstonecraft directly confronts the opposing view. She takes the opponent's positive terms ("delicacy of sentiment," "sweet docility") and calls them "synonymous with epithets of weakness." She then argues that women who are only these things become "objects of contempt." Rather than conceding any value, she redefines those qualities as weaknesses that undermine true virtue.

Why A is incorrect: The author makes no concession. She says she is "despising that weak elegancy" – not moderating it. There is no suggestion of practicing these qualities in moderation.

Why B is incorrect: She does not ignore the opposition. She directly engages with the claimed virtues and refutes them by relabeling them as weaknesses. She also does not focus only on male flattery.

Why D is incorrect: The passage does not accuse men of insincerity nor women of being manipulative. The word "cunning" appears elsewhere in the PDF but in a different context about tyranny, not as a response to this specific viewpoint.

questions.questionHtml: The author uses strong, negative phrases such as "slavish dependence," "weaker vessel," and "objects of contempt." What is the most likely reason she chooses this language?

options.A: To provoke an emotional reaction in her female readers, making them feel ashamed of accepting a passive role and motivated to seek genuine respect through strength.
options.B: To prove that men have deliberately designed social customs to enslave women, and that any woman who complies is complicit in her own oppression.
options.C: To demonstrate that she is angrier at men than at women, and that her primary audience is actually male readers who need to be shamed into changing their behavior.
options.D: To exaggerate the reality of women's situation for dramatic effect, because she believes polite language has failed to convince anyone in the past.

questions.explanationHtml:
The author explicitly states she wants to persuade women to change. Her harsh language serves a rhetorical purpose: to shock her female readers out of complacency. By calling their condition "slavish" and warning that they will become "objects of contempt," she aims to create an emotional response that leads to action. This is consistent with her declared goal of being useful rather than merely elegant.

Why B is incorrect: The passage does not claim men deliberately designed society to enslave women, nor does it say compliant women are "complicit." The tone is more about exposing a system than assigning malicious intent or guilt to individuals.

Why C is incorrect: The author directly addresses "my own sex" at the beginning of the passage. Her primary audience is women, not men. While she criticizes men's language, her purpose is not to shame male readers but to motivate female readers.

Why D is incorrect: The author explicitly rejects exaggeration and artificial feelings. Earlier in the PDF she writes that she aims to be "useful" and will not "dazzle by the elegance of my language" nor "fabricate turgid bombast." She believes her strong terms are accurate descriptions, not dramatic overstatements.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of this passage?

options.A: To list the major civilizations of world history in order to argue that the Negro is the newest and therefore most promising addition to human progress
options.B: To emphasize the painful strangeness of double-consciousness so that readers recognize the Negro's experience as fundamentally different from any other group's struggles
options.C: To argue that the Negro should neither abandon his African heritage nor reject his American identity, but instead merge both into a stronger, truer self
options.D: To explain why the Negro must temporarily prioritize political power and education before attempting any cultural merging of identities

questions.explanationHtml:
The passage's central argument is that the Negro does not want to choose between being African or American. Du Bois explicitly writes, "He would not Africanize America ... He would not bleach his Negro soul." Instead, he "wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American." The verb "to argue" fits because the author is persuading readers to reject a false either‑or choice.

A is incorrect because the mention of Egyptians, Greeks, etc. is only a rhetorical setup, not a historical ranking. The passage never claims the Negro is "most promising."

B is incorrect because while double‑consciousness is described as painful, the passage moves beyond pain to a solution (merging). Du Bois never says the experience is "fundamentally different from any other group's struggles."

D is incorrect because the passage does not prioritize political power or education over merging; it argues for simultaneous integration of both identities. Temporary priority is never mentioned.

questions.questionHtml: How does the author respond to the viewpoint that a person cannot be fully both "a Negro" and "an American" and must eventually choose one identity over the other?

options.A: He dismisses the viewpoint as irrelevant because double‑consciousness is a permanent psychological state that no individual choice can ever resolve
options.B: He partially agrees, suggesting that the Negro should lean toward his American identity while secretly preserving African traditions within the home
options.C: He reframes the debate by arguing that the choice itself is false, and that both identities contain irreplaceable value that must be held together
options.D: He avoids engaging the viewpoint directly and instead focuses entirely on the emotional suffering caused by having two unreconciled ideals

questions.explanationHtml:
Du Bois directly engages the opposing view (that a person must choose one identity). He rejects both extremes: "He would not Africanize America … He would not bleach his Negro soul." Then he offers a different framework: "to merge his double self into a better and truer self." This is a reframing – he shows the choice is false and both identities hold essential value.

A is incorrect because Du Bois does not call the viewpoint "irrelevant." He actively responds to it, and he believes merging is possible, not that double‑consciousness is permanent.

B is incorrect because Du Bois does not "partially agree" with choosing American identity. He explicitly rejects "bleaching his Negro soul," so preserving African traditions only "in private" contradicts his call for full, public recognition.

D is incorrect because Du Bois does not avoid the viewpoint. The second paragraph is a direct counter-argument. Emotional description appears, but it does not replace engagement.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the passage, what can be reasonably inferred about the author's underlying purpose in introducing the metaphor of "double-consciousness" and "two warring ideals in one dark body"?

options.A: To persuade white readers that their society's contempt and pity have caused deep psychological harm, making them morally accountable for changing their behavior
options.B: To help both Negro and white readers understand that the internal conflict of being both Negro and American is not a mark of weakness but a unique source of insight and resilience
options.C: To demonstrate that Negroes possess a form of "second-sight" that makes them better able to judge American society than any white person could
options.D: To suggest that the pain of double-consciousness is so overwhelming that the only practical response is to build separate Negro institutions apart from white society

questions.explanationHtml:
The metaphor of double-consciousness is introduced with the phrase "gifted with second-sight." Although the condition is painful, Du Bois reframes it as a form of insight and strength ("dogged strength alone keeps it from being torn asunder"). The inferred purpose is to change how readers see this conflict – not as weakness, but as a unique perspective that can lead to a merged, stronger self.

A is incorrect because while the passage mentions "amused contempt and pity," the underlying purpose of the metaphor is not to assign blame. The emphasis is on the Negro's resilience and "second-sight," not on white moral accountability.

C is incorrect because "second-sight" is presented as a distinctive perspective, not as proof of superiority. The passage never claims Negroes are "better able to judge ... than any white person."

D is incorrect because the passage explicitly rejects withdrawal: "He would not Africanize America." The metaphor leads toward merging, not separation.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of Thoreau's reference to the philosopher Paley in the final paragraph of the passage?

options.A: To suggest that Paley's theory of "expediency" is valid for small government failures, but not for large-scale injustices like slavery and war.
options.B: To contrast Paley's focus on public inconvenience with a higher moral duty that demands justice regardless of personal or national cost.
options.C: To concede that most people will find Paley's argument more reasonable, while admitting that his own position is only for a heroic few.
options.D: To prove that Paley's philosophy, if followed consistently, would have prevented the American Revolution of 1775.

questions.explanationHtml:
Thoreau brings up Paley not to agree with him but to set up a contrast. Paley argues that citizens should obey the government as long as disobedience would cause more "public inconvenience" than benefit. Thoreau rejects this cost-benefit view entirely. He offers the drowning-man example: even if returning the plank means drowning yourself, you must do it. Likewise, a nation must end slavery and unjust war even if it destroys the nation. The purpose of mentioning Paley is therefore to highlight the conflict between mere expediency (Paley's position) and absolute moral duty (Thoreau's position).

A is incorrect because Thoreau never says Paley's theory is valid for small failures. Earlier he accepts minor taxes as "friction," but he does not credit Paley with that idea. His purpose is not to carve out a partial exception for Paley.

C is incorrect because Thoreau does not concede that Paley is more reasonable for most people. He calls Paley's view incomplete ("never contemplated those cases") and argues forcefully against it, not with reluctance or concession.

D is incorrect because the passage does not use Paley to analyze the American Revolution. The Revolution is mentioned earlier as an example of what people consider justified rebellion, but Paley is brought in to challenge the present-day reluctance to rebel, not to make a historical claim about 1775.

questions.questionHtml: In the first paragraph of the passage, the author states, "I cannot for an instant recognize that political organization as my government which is the slave's government also." How does this statement function within his broader argument?

options.A: It establishes a conditional loyalty: if the government stops supporting slavery, the author would immediately recognize it as his own.
options.B: It serves as a moral boundary that redefines citizenship, allowing the author to later justify refusing allegiance and even encouraging rebellion.
options.C: It shifts the debate from whether a government is efficient to whether it is legitimate in the eyes of an individual's conscience.
options.D: It claims that the American government is unique in history for allowing slavery, unlike the British government during the Revolution.

questions.explanationHtml:
Thoreau's sentence draws a hard line: any government that allows slavery is not his government. This is not a casual opinion; it is the foundation for everything that follows. Once he declares that he does not recognize the state's authority, he can logically argue that refusing to pay taxes, going to jail, and even rebellion are justified. The statement therefore functions as a moral boundary that redefines what it means to be a citizen – citizenship is not automatic but conditional on the state's basic justice. From this boundary, the rest of his argument flows.

A is incorrect because Thoreau never says his recognition is conditional on future reform. He speaks in the present tense ("cannot recognize"). Nowhere does he offer "if they stop slavery, I will recognize them." The statement is an absolute rejection, not a conditional one.

C is incorrect because the phrase "shifts the debate" is too vague. While Thoreau is concerned with conscience, the specific function of this sentence is not to shift a debate but to declare a personal break. More importantly, the sentence directly leads to action (refusal, resistance), not just a theoretical shift.

D is incorrect because the passage does not compare America to Britain regarding slavery. The Revolution of '75 is mentioned to show that people once thought rebellion justified, but Thoreau does not argue that Britain was free of slavery or that America is uniquely evil. This answer imports a historical comparison that the text does not make.

questions.questionHtml: Given the passage as a whole, what is the most likely reason Thoreau includes the hypothetical scenario of the "drowning man" and the "plank"?

options.A: To provide an analogy showing that moral obligations can be absolute and self-destructive, just as ending slavery and war may destroy the nation as it exists.
options.B: To argue that a person who saves his own life by keeping the plank is acting reasonably, but that a truly heroic individual would choose to drown instead.
options.C: To shift the reader's focus from political action (voting, petitioning) to personal, physical action as the only genuine form of resistance.
options.D: To mock Paley's concept of "inconvenience" by inventing an extreme, unrealistic situation where no rational person would follow Paley's advice.

questions.explanationHtml:
The drowning-man example is a direct analogy to the national situation. If you have taken a plank from a drowning person, you must give it back even if that means you drown. Thoreau then applies the same logic: America has taken the freedom of slaves (and invaded Mexico), so it must stop – even if doing so costs the nation its existence. The purpose of the scenario is to illustrate absolute moral duty, where consequences (even death) do not excuse the obligation to do right. This supports his central argument that justice is not a matter of convenience or survival.

B is incorrect because Thoreau does not say keeping the plank is "reasonable." He implies it is a wrong that must be corrected. The phrase "acting reasonably" misrepresents his position; he rejects the idea that self-preservation justifies injustice. There is no sliding scale of heroism – it is simply wrong to keep the plank.

C is incorrect because the drowning-man scenario is not specifically about voting or petitioning. While Thoreau criticizes voting elsewhere in the essay, this paragraph focuses on the moral principle of absolute duty, not on contrasting different forms of political action. The analogy works at the level of personal ethics, not as a comment on protest methods.

D is incorrect because the tone is not mockery. Thoreau is serious, not satirical. He does not present the drowning man as an unrealistic extreme; he presents it as a clear moral test that Paley's philosophy fails. Calling it "unrealistic" misses Thoreau's belief that such absolute choices are real and urgent, especially for a nation facing slavery and war.

questions.questionHtml: What is the primary purpose of this passage?

options.A: To warn readers that all forms of popular government eventually destroy personal security and property rights
options.B: To argue that a republic with representation is better equipped than a pure democracy at controlling the dangerous effects of faction
options.C: To explain why enlightened statesmen cannot be trusted and why citizens should instead govern themselves directly
options.D: To prove that the causes of faction must be removed, even if that means limiting individual liberty

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of correct answer: The author spends most of the passage contrasting pure democracy (which he calls turbulent and short‑lived) with a republic (which uses representation). He states that a republic "promises the cure for which we are seeking." His primary purpose is persuasive: to convince readers that the republican form is superior for controlling faction.

Why A is incorrect: The author attacks only pure democracies, not "all forms of popular government." He explicitly supports republican government, which is also a form of popular government. This answer overgeneralizes his criticism.

Why C is incorrect: The author does argue that enlightened statesmen cannot always be relied upon, but he never concludes that citizens should govern themselves directly. In fact, he rejects direct self‑government (pure democracy) as dangerous.

Why D is incorrect: The author explicitly rejects removing the causes of faction (which would require destroying liberty) as "worse than the disease." This answer states the opposite of his position.

questions.questionHtml: How does the author respond to the claim that enlightened statesmen could solve the problems caused by faction?

options.A: He accepts that statesmen could solve the problem but argues they rarely have enough power to act on their knowledge
options.B: He dismisses the claim as irrelevant because factions only become dangerous when they involve a majority, not a minority
options.C: He rejects the claim by pointing out that statesmen are not always in charge and that self‑interest usually overrides justice
options.D: He partially agrees but adds that statesmen must first convert a pure democracy into a republic before they can be effective

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of correct answer: The author directly addresses this claim in the opening sentences: "It is in vain to say that enlightened statesmen will be able to adjust..." He gives two reasons for rejection: (1) "Enlightened statesmen will not always be at the helm," and (2) "immediate interest... will rarely prevail over... the rights of another." This matches answer C.

Why A is incorrect: The author does not "accept that statesmen could solve the problem." He calls the very idea "in vain" (useless). The claim about power misrepresents his rejection as a conditional acceptance.

Why B is incorrect: The author's response to the statesmen claim appears before his discussion of majority vs. minority factions. He never links the two. This answer invents a connection not present in the text.

Why D is incorrect: The author never mentions converting democracy to a republic in this response. He simply rejects the statesmen argument outright without any partial agreement or added condition.

questions.questionHtml: Based on the passage, the author most likely believes that people who advocate for "pure democracy" are:

options.A: deliberately ignoring the historical evidence that small democracies inevitably become violent and short‑lived
options.B: correct in wanting to protect liberty but wrong in thinking that direct assembly government can control faction
options.C: motivated by a secret desire to abolish property rights and create social chaos
options.D: primarily focused on increasing the number of representatives to better reflect local interests

questions.explanationHtml:
Explanation of correct answer: The author never directly states what pure democracy advocates believe, so you must infer. He calls them "theoretic politicians" who "erroneously supposed" that political equality would lead to equality in possessions and passions. He also opens by calling himself a friend of popular government who values liberty. This shows he thinks they have good intentions (protecting liberty) but are factually wrong about how to control faction.

Why A is incorrect: The author says they "erroneously supposed" — a mistake, not a deliberate ignoring of evidence. "Deliberately ignoring" implies willful dishonesty, which is too harsh and unsupported by the text.

Why C is incorrect: Nothing in the passage suggests secret evil motives. The author argues logically against the system of pure democracy, not against the character of its supporters. This answer is an extreme and unsupported accusation.

Why D is incorrect: The number of representatives and local vs. national interests appear elsewhere in the full Federalist No. X, but that discussion is about republics, not about what pure democracy advocates want. This answer confuses two different sections of the text.
